stops.name: Montpellier, the orphaned niece received
stops.campa: Willehalm-Kyot takes his brother's daughter Condwiramurs into his own household at Montpellier, the city he has favored since his years as duke of the Catalan march, and sets himself as her guardian in the same spirit that once carried Sigune to Hohenburg. He is by any ordinary count an old man now, eighty-six years by the chroniclers' abandoned reckoning, yet the tradition shows him still riding, still building, laying out streets and gardens in Montpellier between the hours he gives to the girl's education and to the grail-account still growing at his writing table.

stops.name: Montpellier, the years of teaching, word of Parzival
stops.campa: Through the years he keeps her, word comes to Montpellier of a young knight named Parzival, questing far to the north and east, who has by report already once failed at Munsalvaesche and turned from God before turning back. Willehalm-Kyot, who found the same castle by a harder road and married into its keeping, recognizes in the reports the shape of his own old search and begins, the tradition says, to ready Condwiramurs for a meeting he has already started arranging in his mind, the last piece of the grail account he means to close not on paper but in the world.

stops.name: Besançon, on the road to Dornachbrugg
stops.campa: In the spring of the year the astronomers of his own school will one day fix past doubt, Willehalm-Kyot leaves Montpellier for the last time with Condwiramurs in his charge, retracing in reverse the road he rode as a young grail-seeker from Provence to the Rhine. He is past ninety by the count the chronicles gave up keeping decades before; the tradition does not trouble itself with the arithmetic, only with the fact of the old man still moving, still delivering what is owed. Through the Burgundian gate at Besançon they pass, then the Jura foothills near Arlesheim where he once found the grail-house itself, and ahead of them both the bridge and town called Dornachbrugg.

stops.name: Dornachbrugg, Whitsun, Condwiramurs given to Parzival
stops.campa: On Whitsunday, a date the tradition's own astronomers calculate against the return of Saturn to its house and confirm centuries later against a planetarium, Willehalm-Kyot brings Condwiramurs across the bridge at Dornach and delivers her into Parzival's hands, closing in a single meeting the account of a niece raised, a search completed, and a debt of kinship paid in full. Parzival, newly named king at Munsalvaesche, receives his wife from the hand of the same old man who once found that grail-house by his own hard road. Willehalm-Kyot has now, by any reckoning but the ordinary chronicles', outlived his own recorded death by thirty-six years to stand at this bridge.
stops.quote: dô der sterne Sâturnus / wider an sîn zil gestuont, / daz wart uns bî der wunden kuont
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival 489,24-26 (Saturn's return marking the season of the wound, the reckoning the tradition credits to Kyot-Willehalm)

stops.name: Montpellier, the return, and the writing that becomes the source
stops.campa: Willehalm-Kyot rides back to Montpellier alone, the office of guardian finished, and takes up for the last time the account he has kept in fragments since Le Verdus: Alischanz and Gyburc, the Arabic manuscript and Flegetanis's starwriting, Munsalvaesche and Schoysiane, Sigune's leash and Condwiramurs's wedding, the whole ninety-year weight of it set down as the true report only its own witness could give. He commits it to an oral transmission that will run through the Provençal courts for three and a half centuries before a German poet named Wolfram finds it and swears, against his own age's doubt, that he says nothing but what his master Kyot has spoken.
stops.quote: Ob von Troys meister Cristjân / disem mære hât unreht getân, / daz mac wol zürnen Kyôt, / der uns diu rehten mære enbôt
